en: *Mahāparinirvāṇa-śāstra*, one fascicle;
composed by Vasubandhu,
translated by the śramaṇa Dharmabodhi.
I prostrate to the ocean of pure awakening, who maintains the gateway to the nectar of immortality;
I also pay homage to the inconceivable treasury of self-nature purity.
To the gateways of the various perfections that save the world, and to the path of the true reality toward which one correctly proceeds—homage to them!
Furthermore, as he studied according to his studies, realized the true meaning in accordance with the Dharma,
and out of compassion for the long-deluded masses of sentient beings, he transmitted [the teachings] to the world with a heart of sorrow.
From this beginning until the point where blood flowed and drenched the ground, it is called the section on the "Inconceivable Supernatural Powers of Counter-Demonstration."
The two chapters, "Cunda" and "Lamentation," are titled the Section on Accomplishing the Spiritual Lineage and Dispelling Attachments.
From the threefold address below up to the end of the "Chapter on the Questions of the Great Assembly," it is titled the Section on the True Meaning of the Right Dharma.
The five practices and ten merits are called the section on the cultivation of skillful means;
the "Lion’s Roar" chapter is called the section on entering realization by departing from all negligence;
and the "Kāśyapa" chapter is called the section on skillfully maintaining the teaching through the light of compassion.
The "Kauṇḍinya Chapter" is titled to manifest the aspect of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bhāga*).
Why is it that one attains a long-lived, adamantine, indestructible body?
Kāśyapa asked this because he wished for all sentient beings to hear it together with him.
The intended meaning of the answer is: "I have attained long life because I have cultivated the three karmas.
How can you ask about a vajra-like indestructible body?
All sentient beings are subject to decay; how then can one attain indestructibility?"
As previously practiced, one attains non-destruction.
What is firm power? Because the mind is free from conceptual discrimination, it attains firmness.
Because there is neither coming nor going, it is long-lived;
because it is ineffable, it is indestructible;
because it is without movement, it is firm and solid.
"How does one attain long life? Because one attains a vajra-like indestructible body, one attains long life.
"How is it indestructible? Because one has attained firm and solid power, it is indestructible.
Kāśyapa asked this because sentient beings are not of a single type; he asked so that the characteristics of the Dharma might not be exhausted.
I pray that the Buddha will reveal this subtle mystery and explain it extensively for the sake of all sentient beings.
What is meant by "subtle mystery"?

That there is a Buddha outside the body is not a mystery; that there is a Buddha within the body is also not a mystery; and that he neither exists nor does not exist is likewise not a mystery. Because sentient beings themselves are the Buddha, it is a subtle mystery.
In what sense are sentient beings Buddhas?
Sentient beings are neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both, nor neither; therefore, sentient beings are Buddhas.
How do they attain vastness and become a refuge for all beings?
Why is it called "vast"?

Because there is no mark of consciousness, because there is nothing that is not Buddha, because there is no conduct that is not pure, and because there is no virtue that is not fulfilled; therefore, it is said that he acts as a refuge for all beings.
To see those who rely upon Śākyamuni as merely relying [upon him] is not called true reliance.
According to the interpretation of the Lesser Vehicle, he causes sentient beings to rely [upon him] out of compassion;

yet in reality, he is not an Arhat. As for those who are equal to an Arhat: while the former teaching stated that he was born in the royal palace and attained Arhatship there, the present teaching states that the royal palace was not his birthplace and the Twin Trees were not his place of extinction.
How is it that one who is not an Arhat is equal to an Arhat?
Kāśyapa had not yet received the Buddha’s teaching and did not inquire about the four reliances.
Question:

If the Tathāgata was neither born in the royal palace nor extinguished at the Twin Trees, having naturally attained the precepts without depending on the four fruits of the path, he is truly not an arhat.
How then could the Tathāgata be equal to an arhat?
The commentary states:
If the Tathāgata were truly an arhat, then the four reliances could be equated with those of an arhat.
Since the Buddha is not truly an arhat, how can it be said that he is equal to an arhat?
The body of Śākyamuni has two names:
the first is "One Who Should Come" (Āgantuka),
and the second is "Bodhisattva of True Practice" (Bodhisattva-samyak-pratipatti).

As for what is called "correspondence": from the World of Lotus Treasury, the Buddha Mahāvyūha manifested as a crown prince, appearing to be born in a royal palace and to pass away at the twin śāla trees; this is the dharma of the bodhisattva’s playful manifestation.
Regarding the second "true" one: since he comes from nowhere, how could he be equal to an Arhat?
The Buddha has two kinds of names:
first, the True Buddha, who manifests in forms identical to Śrāvakas and Arhats; yet the Buddha is not actually a Śrāvaka, so how could he be equal to the four types of Śrāvakas?
If there had truly been Arhats previously, one could say, "I am equal to the Arhats";
but since there were no Arhats before, and it was my own self that created what is called an "Arhat," how can I be said to be equal?
Furthermore, you explain that the body of Śāriputra was named an Arhat; how then can a Bodhisattva of the Stage of Nature (gotrabhūmi) be equal to an Arhat?
Second, a Bodhisattva of True Practice (pratipannaka) should also come, and he too is capable of manifesting as a Buddha.
If Śākyamuni were truly an Arhat, one could say they are equal;
but since Śākyamuni was never an Arhat, how can they be said to be equal?
Therefore, it is the Bodhisattva of the Stage of Right Nature who is the Arhat; yet this Bodhisattva is not actually a Buddha. How, then, can an Arhat be equal to a Buddha?
If Śākyamuni were truly an arhat, one could say they are equal;
but since Śākyamuni has never been an arhat, how can they be equal?

Therefore, it is the Bodhisattva of True Practice who is the arhat. Thus, his birth in the royal palace and his passing away between the twin śāla trees are both manifestations of his skillful play (*vikrīḍita*). These are deeds performed by the Bodhisattva; previously, there was in fact no arhat. It is because of my transformation that sentient beings attain arhatship, and for this reason, I manifest as an arhat.
The second transformation bodhisattva from the Lotus Treasury World is no different from me; therefore, although he is not actually an arhat, he is equal to an arhat.
If I were truly an arhat, then the bodhisattva could indeed be my equal.
Those who grasp at me as being an arhat do not understand the transformative penetration of the dharma-characteristics of a bodhisattva; all such views are unreal.
Explaining the four reliances:
the Stage of Joy is the first reliance;
the sixth stage is the second reliance.
The eighth stage serves as the third reliance;
the Dharma-cloud stage serves as the fourth reliance.
As for the transformation of śrāvakas, since their [realized] severance was merely illusory and they were never truly arhats, how could they be equal [to those on the stages]?
A Bodhisattva is called a Dharma-Buddha and is also called a Condition-Buddha (Pratyaya-Buddha).
What is meant by a Dharma-Buddha?
Because they are born from the Dharma, and because they practice the Dharma and thereby attain vision, they are called Dharma-Buddhas.
What is meant by "taking the Buddha as an object"?
Because there is an object, one sees; this is called taking the Buddha as an object.
Question:
If Kāśyapa’s mind had understood it by himself, there would have been no need for him to ask such a question;
if he had never heard or seen it, how could he have asked such a question? Answer:
Kāśyapa is one of the twelve youths; it is through the empowerment and instruction of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual power that he is able to ask.
That which Kāśyapa asks is precisely *nirvāṇa*, and there is nothing else external to it.
"How does one know that the celestial Māra creates obstacles for the assembly?
Explanation:
This Kāśyapa is asking specifically about the Tathāgata’s own person, not regarding the future.
How is this known? Sentient beings themselves do not have faith in their own bodies; how then could external demons come to create obstacles?
Now that the Tathāgata has just attained Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree and the True Dharma is about to flourish, Māra fears losing his followers and therefore creates these obstacles.
How is it that the Tamer (Vināyaka) joyfully proclaims the True Dharma?
What is meant by "Tamer"?

Ordinary beings possess no knowledge; they hear that the Mahāyāna is the Mahāyāna, they hear that the Hīnayāna is the Hīnayāna, they hear that suffering is suffering, and they hear that pleasure is pleasure. Why, then, are they called "Tamers"?

To speak of suffering where there is no suffering, to speak of pleasure where there is no pleasure, to speak of permanence where there is no permanence, and to speak of the Great where one previously spoke of the Small—this is not called "speaking the Truth with a joyful mind," nor is it called "being a Tamer."

Now it is taught that impermanence is not [merely] impermanent, suffering and pleasure are not [merely] suffering or pleasure, and there is neither coming nor going; this is called the teaching of the True Reality.
Perfectly and excellently accomplished, it proclaims the four inversions.

Regarding "perfectly accomplishing what is correct and wholesome": when a bodhisattva practices the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) and the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*), there is nothing that is not impartial; this is called "correctness and wholesomeness within characteristics. In the practice of a bodhisattva, there is nothing that is not correct and wholesome.
Because śrāvakas possess the distinction between self and other, they are not called "rightly good";
because bodhisattvas are free from such distinctions, they are called "rightly good.
Regarding the second point on being "rightly good": the former teachings were not definitive, and thus the śrāvakas did not fully accomplish them.
Now, the principle of Nirvāṇa is correct: being without coming or going, and without birth or cessation, it is called "perfectly and rightly accomplished.
Second, from the stage of Joy (Pramuditā) up to the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā) stage, this is called "accomplished."

He expounds upon the four perversions: the śrāvakas claim that "self, permanence, bliss, and purity" are perversions, while the Buddha claims that "suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self" are perversions; yet the śrāvakas' "suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self" and the Buddha's "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" are likewise both perversions.
The Buddha’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, as well as the suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self of sentient beings—these too are inversions.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata speak of the four inversions?
He speaks of them for the sake of the śrāvakas.

To correctly explain that the four inversions are themselves non-inversions, and that there are no external dharmas that are either inverted or non-inverted—this is called "joyfully speaking the True Dharma.
As a sutra says: "To speak of dharmas as neither existent nor non-existent—this is called the True Dharma."
How is it that Bodhisattvas are able to see the nature that is difficult to see?

Kāśyapa has two intentions: first, he wishes to cause all sentient beings to know that Buddha-nature exists; [second, he wishes to cause them to realize that Buddha-nature is not something newly produced].
Second, they do not wish to cause others to see the Buddha-nature.
Why do they not wish for them to know and see it?
It is because they desire to cause the Tathāgata to have a profound understanding of the Buddha-nature.
For what reason is it called "profound"?
Because the Buddha-nature cannot be made, constructed, cultivated, or attained, it is called profound.
The Śrāvakas, being narrow-minded and lacking ultimate realization, are unable to see it.
The Bodhisattva practices compassion and universal salvation, yet does not seek to be seen.
Because he acts for the sake of sentient beings and because he is bound [by vows], he is said to be "difficult to see.
Second interpretation:

The Buddha-nature is not a phenomenon that can be seen; because it is the seer and the seen, the knower and the known, the practitioner and the practiced, it is called the "nature difficult to see" for those who are able to see.
How does one understand the meaning of the full syllables and the half syllables?
The "half-syllables" refer to the gradual teaching; the "full-syllables" refer to *nirvāṇa*. Because it is a teaching that brings [the goal] to fulfillment, it is called the full-syllable.
Because it encompasses all the merits of the fruit of the Buddha's teaching, it is called the full-syllable.
Because the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not complete, they are called "half-letters.
Nirvāṇa is called both "sudden" and "gradual.
Now, in discussing nirvāṇa, it is "complete" within the context of the relative relationship between the two truths.
Because practice may be either complete or incomplete, it is called the "Gradual Teaching";
because principle is neither complete nor incomplete,
Nirvana is named the "Gradual Teaching" and is contrasted with the "Half-Syllables."
Nirvāṇa is termed the Sudden Teaching.

Regarding the second point concerning "full" and "partial," these are the deluded conceptualizations of sentient beings; in principle, there is neither fullness nor non-fullness. Therefore, it is said that Nirvāṇa is the Gradual Teaching.
How is it that bodhisattvas are able to see the nature that is difficult to see?
Is it that they see only phenomena (*dharma*)?
Furthermore, what is meant by "understanding the meaning of the full syllables (*pūrṇākṣara*) and the half-syllables (*ardhākṣara*)?"
Now there is neither seeing nor not-seeing.
How does one practice the noble conduct together?
It is like the śarabha bird.
The Tathāgata was born in a royal palace, took a wife, and had children; yet he also renounced the world and lived as a śrāvaka.

This is like the sārasa birds, which form such a flock that they cannot be distinguished from one another. Because the Noble One, the Tathāgata, practices and acts in the same way as all sentient beings, it is said: "How does he practice the noble conduct? Like the sārasa birds."
The second interpretation:
Form constitutes a noble one; for śrāvakas, both form and mind constitute a noble one, whereas for bodhisattvas, neither mind nor form constitutes a noble one.
To say that they possess mind and form is why they are not noble ones.

The physical forms of Śrāvaka noble ones are common [to ordinary beings], whereas Bodhisattva noble ones possess no blue, yellow, red, or white mental consciousness; since ordinary beings possess mental consciousness as a principle while noble ones are without it, they are called "noble ones" (ārya).
The term "sārasa bird" is a general name; it is like the Tathāgata being inseparable from all sentient beings.
The "kalaviṅka" is a metaphor for nirvāṇa distinguishing itself from all sentient beings, thereby returning to the perspective of the śrāvaka.
The Bodhisattva knows that the Tathāgata is without distinction from all sentient beings; therefore, it is called "common.
It is understood as the relinquishing of characteristics.
Before the Tathāgata appeared in the world, there was the relinquishing of the characteristics of ordinary persons and sages.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, all sentient beings do not abandon one another;
this is the intention of the śrāvaka.

As for bodhisattvas not abandoning one another: whether the Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, they do not abandon one another. Whether the Tathāgata appears in the world or not, they remain inseparable.

In the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), there is no suffering, emptiness, impermanence, or non-self; in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there is no impermanence, suffering, non-self, or impurity. Some say:
there is no conventional truth, but there is permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
They offer a superficial understanding of the principles. Furthermore, some say:
"Existence is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and non-existence is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)."
"Both existent and non-existent" is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); "neither existent nor non-existent" is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Because that which is neither existent nor non-existent has no further external phenomena, it is called the "common practice of the noble ones" (ārya-caryā).
The *kālaṃji* flower, the sun and moon, Venus, and Jupiter—how are the sun and moon defined?
These "sun and moon" are metaphors for the way ordinary persons perceive the rising and setting of the sun and moon; noble ones have never seen such rising or setting.
Second, the śrāvaka sees the Buddha born in the royal palace and pass away between the twin śāla trees;
the bodhisattva has never seen him born in the royal palace or enter nirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees.
Third, because the sun and moon have set, Venus and Jupiter emerge, causing people of the world to give rise to strange notions.
When the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas emerge; since the Dharma is distinct from the Tathāgata, it is said that "the stars have emerged."
Sentient beings falsely perceive the sun, moon, and Jupiter as having rising and setting, yet in reality they have no rising or setting;
sentient beings see the Tathāgata as having birth and extinction, yet the Tathāgata truly has no birth or extinction.
How is it that one who has not yet generated the resolve is called a bodhisattva?

Śrāvakas may have generated the resolve or not; pratyekabuddhas likewise may have generated it or not; and bodhisattvas also may have generated it or not—it is these three types of bodhisattvas who are said to have "generated the resolve."
What is meant by "arousing the mind"?
Because the fruit is distinct, it can be termed "arousing the mind.
From the initial teaching onwards, there are among sentient beings those who do and those who do not arouse this mind.
In the ancient teachings, what is called "setting forth" is not truly termed setting forth.
Why is it not termed setting forth?
Because if one perceives a Buddha as something distinct that can be attained or sought after, such differentiation is not termed setting forth.
What is meant by "arousing"?
It is now explained that because they are permeated by the principle of signless nirvāṇa, all beings are caused to arouse [the aspiration for awakening]; this is what is called "arousing.
This is because there is no distinction among śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas regarding whether they have aroused it or not.

To say that one is called a bodhisattva even before generating the aspiration for enlightenment is because nirvāṇa impartially illuminates all; therefore, all who have not yet generated the aspiration are called bodhisattvas.
Kāśyapa, for what reason do you ask how one who has not yet resolved their mind can be called a bodhisattva?
One who has resolved their mind beholds the sun and moon;
one who has not resolved their mind does not behold the sun and moon.
Those who have awakened the resolve perceive the eternally abiding [Tathāgata], while those who have not awakened the resolve do not see him.

As previously stated, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, there are those who awaken the resolve and those who do not; those who awaken the resolve see him, while those who do not awaken it do not see him.
Now, in this parinirvāṇa, there is impartial illumination; its arising is both arising and non-arising.
How does one attain fearlessness amidst the great assembly?
Because the Bodhisattva’s supramundane compassion is impartial, they do not destroy the marks of sentient beings.
Regarding fearlessness: the bodhisattva is fearless, and sentient beings are likewise fearless.
Why are sentient beings fearless?
Because when the bodhisattva appears in the world, they do not destroy the marks of sentient beings; therefore, sentient beings are also fearless.

When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he employs the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity with impartiality and without distinction; regarding no one—whether devas, Māras, non-Buddhists, or even icchantikas—as anything other than his only child, he remains free from fear.
Why do sentient beings have nothing to fear?
Because all sentient beings regard the Tathāgata as their parents, they have nothing to fear.
Why is one called an icchantika?
One who does not recognize the Buddha and does not recognize the internal or external paths is called an icchantika.
Question:
What is the difference between an icchantika, who does not recognize the internal or external, and a bodhisattva?
The explanation says:
A bodhisattva does not kill because they do not perceive "internal" or "external," whereas an icchantika kills because they lack such perception.
This is just as no one can speak of any fault in Jāmbūnada gold.
Explanation:
This refers to the meaning of "harmonizing the assembly.
There are four kinds of Jambūnada gold.
What are these four? First, blue;
second, yellow.
Third, red; fourth, purple-gold. Blue represents the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas);
yellow represents the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; red represents the bodhisattvas of the six pāramitās; and purple-gold represents the Tathāgata.
Jāmbūnada gold also possesses four kinds of colors—blue, yellow, red, and white.
Second, although worldly fine objects may be handsome, they still possess deficiencies.
Jambu-river gold is not like this object; its faults cannot be described.

This is analogous to the Tathāgata’s attainment of nirvāṇa, as well as the various śrāvakas, non-Buddhists, and bodhisattvas of the six pāramitās—just like Jambu-river gold, their faults cannot be described.
Just as purple-polished gold possesses all colors, so too does nirvāṇa encompass the celestial māras and non-Buddhists, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas of the six pāramitās.
Why is this so? Because there is no other distinct phenomenon beyond this.
It is like the purple-polished gold that possesses every perfection; its various colors are ineffable.
Because śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, the six pāramitās, and the various heterodox paths exist, it cannot be described.
The principle of nirvāṇa is not a phenomenon of blue, yellow, red, or white, yet because it is also blue, yellow, red, and white, it is said to be inexpressible.
If there were blue, yellow, red, or white, one could speak of their faults; however, since these colors have never existed, they cannot be spoken of.
How is it that one dwells in a turbid world yet remains unstained, like a lotus flower?
The "defiled world" refers to the five defilements (pañca-kaṣāya).
What are the five defilements? They are the defilement of the eon (kalpa-kaṣāya) and the defilement of afflictions (kleśa-kaṣāya).

Śākyamuni appeared in the five turbidities; he was born in a royal palace and had a wife and children, and gold, silver, the seven treasures, and all manner of wealth—all these are termed "turbidities.
Because he was not defiled by them, it is said that he dwells in a world of turbidity without being stained, like a lotus flower.
The vehicles of the second and third [turnings] are called turbid; "gold" refers to *nirvāṇa*, which cannot be defiled by the three vehicles, and is therefore termed "unstained.
How is it that while abiding amidst afflictions (*kleśa*), one cannot be stained by those afflictions?
Just as a physician treats various illnesses without being defiled by those illnesses, Kāśyapa’s intention in asking this question was based on the Tathāgata:
although there are the afflictions of the triple world and the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the Tathāgata, having appeared in the world, is not defiled by them.
All sentient beings are defiled by the afflictions of the three realms and the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Second, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as those practicing the six *pāramitās*, calculate that there are afflictions to be severed and a Buddha-fruit to be attained; for this reason, they too are defiled by afflictions.
Because Bodhisattvas of the ten stages practice the penetration of great wisdom, they are not defiled by afflictions.
However, even a fourth-stage Great Bodhisattva, when looking toward the fruit, is still defiled by afflictions.
Present Nirvāṇa is not something obtained through cause and effect; therefore, it is not defiled.

Even the fifth teaching of the Four Noble Truths, up to the Prajñāpāramitā and the Lotus Sūtra, are said to be defiled by afflictions (*kleśa*). However, the principle of present Nirvāṇa is without movement, without gain or loss, and without arising or ceasing; therefore, it is not defiled, just as a physician who treats various illnesses is not defiled by those illnesses.

When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he begins with the three refuges and the five precepts, and proceeds up to the bodhisattva precepts; through such gradual teaching as even a single snap of the fingers or a slight bowing of the head, he cures the illnesses of sentient beings. Because he understands afflictions, he is not defiled by them.
Because sentient beings do not understand afflictions, they are constantly defiled by illness.
The second sequential teaching is also called "Treating the Illnesses of Sentient Beings.
The third is called the "Teaching of Power," wherein all are subdued through supernatural transformations and emanations; this is also called "Treating the Illnesses of Sentient Beings."
The fourth [teaching] now speaks of *nirvāṇa* to remedy the defects of the previous distinct teachings; it is also called the "treatment for all ailments.
What is meant by "ailment"?
The state in which all sentient beings have not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment is called an ailment.
Seeing the sixteen-foot [Buddha] form inspire the aspiration for enlightenment, yet understanding that it is not the sixteen-foot form itself that causes the aspiration to arise;
because Nirvana illuminates with equality, causing this aspiration to be generated, it is called "healing all ailments."
Within the great ocean of birth and death, how does one become a master mariner?
The three realms are called "birth and death," and the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is also called "birth and death.
Why is it called "birth and death"?
The Dharma of the Tathāgata can deliver sentient beings so that they do not undergo birth and death; therefore, it is said that he acts as a helmsman within the great ocean of birth and death.
The second [teaching], the sixteen-foot [form] preaching the sequential Dharma, even up to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, is also called the "Dharma of Birth and Death."

Now, in explaining nirvana as being without coming or going, and without arising or ceasing, he delivers beings from the teachings concerning prior birth and death; therefore, he is named the "Mariner.
First, he explains that the *zhànglù* (sixteen-foot) body is neither born nor dies, and that the teaching itself is without arising or ceasing.
The second [category], those of one zhang and six chi as well as their teachings, are also subject to birth and death; nirvana is without arising or ceasing.
Regarding the third, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, who is able to deliver others from birth and death?
Only the great bodhisattvas can deliver others from birth and death.
Even the fourth stage of bodhisattvas cannot cross over; it is the principle of Great Nirvana that can cross over birth and death.

This is like a worldly boatman who is skilled in expedient means and knows the perils of the sea: the great ocean of afflictions is the sea, the three realms are the boat, and the Tathāgata, through various expedient means, teaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles as the boatman.
The mariner of the world points to the cause and points to the fruit as sentient beings board the ship;

the Tathāgata, through skillful means, teaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, speaking of causes and fruits, yet declaring that even those who have emerged from the three realms are still within birth and death. For this reason, he takes the three realms themselves as the ship.
The gradual teaching is called "the boatman" because it delivers sentient beings across the cycle of birth and death;
the Lotus Sūtra takes the myriad practices as its boatman.
Now, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, nirvana itself is the boat—being free from birth and death—so why does it point to being defiled by illness?
Furthermore, within the great ocean of birth and death, how does one act as a boatman?
One goes before [the wayfarers] to eliminate afflictions.
Moreover, acting as a boatman within the great ocean of afflictions, one ferries others across to reach the other shore.
"How does one abandon birth and death?
Like a snake shedding its old skin.
Kāśyapa asked:
The Tathāgata appears in the world amidst birth and death, yet now he speaks of the path to entering nirvāṇa.
I am neither born nor do I die; like a snake shedding its old skin, I am without arising or ceasing.
What was previously taught in the sixteen-foot form pertains to the dharma of birth and death; what is spoken now is that nirvāṇa is non-extinguishing.
The previous sequential teaching— that this teaching is without principle, like a snake shedding its old skin, being neither beneficial nor meritorious— is now superseded by Nirvana,
which is without arising and without cessation, and thus does not subvert the teaching.
Second, regarding all sentient beings, from those who speak to those who do not speak, all that possesses form and category exists merely as empty names; only nirvana is the true principle.
How does one contemplate the Three Jewels as being like the celestial wish-fulfilling tree?
The Three Jewels are called the "standard" (*koṭi*); when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he manifests the existence of the Three Jewels.

Because the Three Jewels exist, one receives the three refuges and attains the five precepts; furthermore, one attains the snapping of fingers [as a sign of attainment], and one attains whatever is cultivated according to one's will and whatever is obtained according to one's will.
The Tathāgata is also called the "Wish-Fulfilling Triple Gem," and is also called the "Wish-Fulfilling Tathāgata" and the "Wish-Fulfilling for Sentient Beings.
What is meant by "wish-fulfilling for sentient beings"?

It is because they may, according to their wishes, receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, up to and including the state of a Bodhisattva, and all thereby obtain their karmic rewards; therefore, it is called "wish-fulfilling for sentient beings."
The Tathāgata is "as one wishes" (yirui) because he responds to the capacities and inspirations of sentient beings; thus he is called "as one wishes.

Now, regarding "Nirvāṇa as one wishes," it means that all suffering and pleasure, good and evil, are none other than the principle (li); therefore it is called "as one wishes. Thus it is said that contemplating the Triple Gem is like the *kalpavṛkṣa* (the wish-fulfilling tree).

For example, in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), there is a tree that can provide whatever the various devas desire; therefore, it is called the "Wish-Fulfilling Tree" (Kalpavṛkṣa).
Because these devas have practiced spiritual conduct for a long time, they have brought forth this tree as a result of their merit.

The Three Jewels are also like this: because sentient beings have practiced for a long time, they elicit a response in the form of the six-cubit body; therefore, the Three Jewels are said to be like the *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree) of the devas.
If the three vehicles lacked intrinsic nature, how could it be said that the three vehicles are not [ultimately] real? Why would the Tathāgata preach a single dharma?
Regarding the three vehicles: because they correspond to the faculties of sentient beings, it is said that a single sound is preached, yet understood according to their respective types.
When the Tathāgata speaks of the three vehicles, this is not called "preaching" [in the ultimate sense], for he follows the faculties of sentient beings; thus there are the small and the great.
Although the Tathāgata speaks of the three vehicles, this is not his original intention.
What is the Tathāgata’s original intention? It is nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa’s intention in questioning was: "If the three vehicles have no intrinsic nature, how can they be taught?
The Tathāgata’s intention in answering was: "All Buddhas do not teach the three vehicles for the sake of sentient beings."

The true reality (*dharmatā*) of nirvāṇa now is such that it is not small in its smallness, nor large in its largeness; one should know that the teachings of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) constitute a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), and therein is no distinction between great and small.

In the third discourse on the principle of nirvāṇa, neither "great" nor "small" is spoken of; rather, because the wisdom of sentient beings differs, the teachings differ. Since there is no differentiation of great or small within the principle itself, one may speak of "great" and "small" [only in reference to the capacity of the recipients].
That which was previously described as differentiation is, in truth, non-differentiation; there is nothing else external to it.
It is just as when pleasure has not yet arisen—how could it be called "experiencing pleasure"?
Kāśyapa then asked:
Sentient beings do not know bliss; how, then, can one speak of experiencing bliss?
Ordinary persons have suffering but no bliss, whereas Bodhisattvas have bliss but no suffering.
Why is there bliss?
Because the Bodhisattva’s wisdom-penetration reaches the ultimate fruit, he knows pleasure; because sentient beings do not know this, they experience suffering.

The Bodhisattva, knowing the fruit, says that what is called the Bodhisattva’s pleasure is not truly pleasure, and what is called the suffering of sentient beings is not truly suffering, for both are equally illusory.
Nirvana is without suffering and without pleasure; it is called "Great Bliss. Therefore, since pleasure has not yet arisen, how can it be called "experiencing pleasure"?
Question:
When the Tathāgata preached the Dharma in the Śāla grove, why did he not exclusively teach the precepts for maintaining merit?
"Those who do not obtain the merit of the precepts are non-Buddhists; their precepts are not those of the Buddha.
The intent of the Buddha’s reply was that what was previously described as the "mixed teaching" is itself nirvana; there is no separate nirvana for non-Buddhists.
How do bodhisattvas attain an indestructible assembly?

First, those who understand the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, the six pāramitās of bodhisattvas, and even the non-Buddhists as having distinctions between self and other, and as having something to be attained or realized, are said to have a "destructible assembly."

Second, regarding the bodhisattva’s secret practice and secret teaching: knowing the root-natures of sentient beings, one is called "destructive" because one does not destroy the marks of sentient beings.
That which the bodhisattva does not destroy is what can truly be destroyed; that which cannot be destroyed is not the domain of a bodhisattva.
Because they are able to perform such actions without contradicting the characteristics of the Dharma, they are called an "indestructible assembly.
Third, because Bodhisattvas know that nirvana has no blue, yellow, red, or white, and possesses neither "this" nor "that," they are called an "indestructible assembly."
Regarding the fourth "indestructible," because the principle of *nirvāṇa* is neither attained nor realized, and neither created nor made, one obtains the assembly of the indestructible.
Fifth, the true principle does not destroy sentient beings, and sentient beings do not destroy the principle.
Why is this so? Sentient beings are the principle; outside of this principle, there are no further sentient beings. Therefore, one does not destroy the multitude.
How then can one act as eyes and a guide for those born blind?
Kāśyapa asked:
"In what way does one act as an eye and a guide?

One interpretation is that those who understand the previous teachings on the six *pāramitās* for *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, yet do so according to their characteristics, are called "blind from birth."

The Tathāgata understands that for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, if the six pāramitās had ever been something attained, they could not be opened; it is because this dharma was never previously existent that it can be opened.
For example, it is like a blind person who does not know blue, yellow, red, or white; if someone were to speak of blue, yellow, red, or white to them, they would become even more confused.
If one says there is no blue, yellow, red, or white, this accords with what [the blind person] understands and is called an "opening analogy."
Those of the three vehicles clearly understand that there are causes and effects, and that there are distinctions between attainment and non-attainment.
Now, regarding the discourse on nirvāṇa, if one perceives it as having length or brevity, or as being attained or not attained, one will become increasingly deluded.
It is said that Nirvana has no blue, yellow, red, or white; because it is without attainment or realization, and without long or short, it is called the "opening of the cause.

The practice of the Way, the observance of precepts, and the giving of alms by the sixteen-foot [Buddha] are not the cause; rather, the Buddha-nature which is without attainment and without cultivation is what is called the cause.
All sentient beings regard those of the three vehicles as the Dharma, yet those of the three vehicles are called "blue-blind.
Not only are those of the three vehicles blue-blind, but all sentient beings are likewise blue-blind.
The Dharma is neither visible nor invisible, neither openable nor unopenable, neither attainable nor unattainable; it is through teaching that one speaks of "blindness on the path.
In principle, there is no blindness on the path, nor is there non-blindness; therefore, speaking of blindness on the path or non-blindness does not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma.
If these two aspects exist, one may say that it has neither been existent nor non-existent.
Why then do we speak of existence and non-existence, non-non-existence and non-non-non-existence? Because opening and non-opening are both non-contradictory, it is called "opening."
"How is it that you manifest many heads? We pray that the Great Seer will explain this.
Kāśyapa’s intention in asking was this: the Tathāgata initially taught various manifold heads; why now, in the *Nirvāṇa*, is there only one, without a second?
The Tathāgata replied: "It is not that I have many heads; rather, because sentient beings in the past practiced many faculties (*indriya*), I speak of having many heads.
Therefore, it is said that I manifest many heads.
Second, the multiplicity of dharmas.
Why is it called "many"?
Because the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are such, they are shown as having many heads;
this is the reason why "many" is spoken of in the third [section].
If this Dharma existed, it could be called "much spoken of";
since this Dharma has never existed, it is therefore not "much spoken of.
Such is the principle and characteristic of the fourth, Nirvana; it is neither much nor not much.
The fifth truth is that, from beginning to end, it is neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, whether one speaks of it or does not speak of it, there is no obstruction.
*Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, one fascicle.
